Chapter 8: The Illusion of Objectivity—Why “Neutral” Algorithms Aren’t
You know, it’s really tempting to think that algorithms are completely impartial. Almost like they’re this magic escape hatch from all the messy parts of human decision-making.
But the truth? It’s way more complicated than that.
Every single model out there is built on a series of choices. Think about it—someone decides what data goes in, what outcomes matter most, or even what risks to avoid. And all those decisions? They’re shaped by the values, assumptions, and even blind spots of the people building the models, no matter how hard they try to stay neutral.
Picture a tech company that wants to improve its hiring process. The team builds a model to predict which candidates will do well on the job. They pick out things like education, work history, maybe some test scores—believing these are fair, objective measures.
But here’s the catch: every one of those choices can carry hidden biases. Maybe the model starts favoring people from certain schools, or with specific backgrounds. And, over time, instead of getting a more diverse team, the company actually ends up with less diversity.
Now, let’s look at policing. Some departments use software trained on old arrest records, hoping it’ll help predict future crime. But those records? They’re already shaped by years of policy and practice—who gets stopped, who gets charged, who even gets noticed.
The algorithm ends up acting like a mirror, reflecting all those old injustices, rather than being a neutral judge.
Even in healthcare, you see the same pattern. Imagine a hospital using a model to figure out which patients are most at risk for complications. If the data comes mostly from insurance claims, what happens to people without steady coverage? Their risks might get overlooked. The predictions end up being less accurate for folks who are poor, uninsured, or on the margins.
This illusion of objectivity is powerful. It lets decision-makers trust the model, believe the outcomes are fair—even when bias is sneaking in. Most of the time, people don’t even notice all the little ways it happens. It’s not just about the data itself, but the very questions the model is built to answer.
For the people on the receiving end, it can feel totally bewildering. A job applicant wonders why they never get a call back. A patient is denied extra care, and there’s no clear explanation. To them, the model’s decisions feel random—almost like they’re disconnected from reality.
So, what’s the real takeaway here? Neutrality isn’t automatic. It’s not something you just get by plugging in data and letting the algorithm run. It’s actually a goal—one you have to work toward, over and over. That means testing models, challenging their assumptions, and always keeping an eye on whether the outcomes are truly fair.
The answer isn’t to throw out algorithms altogether. Instead, it’s about recognizing their limits—being honest about the ways bias can find its way in. When we do that, we can start building models that are more transparent, more accountable, and ultimately, more just.
